documents.unit: Academic Senate, Work Group on Generative AI
documents.title: GenAI Guidance for Instructors (2025)
documents.summary: Academic Senate guidance to all Berkeley faculty. It sets no campus-wide rule: it recommends a syllabus statement, lays out arguments for prohibiting, allowing or requiring GenAI, supplies three sample statements, and gives advice on access, citation, enforcement and the Code of Student Conduct.
documents.stance_why: The guidance reminds faculty of 'their authority over courses and curriculum' and offers three sample statements (Full AI, Some AI, No AI) that 'Instructors should modify', so the decision is delegated to instructors with named tiers.

units.why: States the purpose and audience of the guidance: a Senate-issued framework for all teaching faculty, so it sets scope and purpose (P56). It informs rather than binds.
units.anchor: The Berkeley Division of the Academic Senate wishes to provide the following guidance to all
units.policy: The Berkeley Division of the Academic Senate wishes to provide the following guidance to all faculty (all titles with a teaching function).

units.why: Says when the guidance was developed ('met during the Spring 2025 semester'), which describes how the policy was made (P84).
units.anchor: The working group met during the Spring 2025 semester.

units.why: Names the consultation inputs (Senate session, Student Pulse Survey, faculty feedback) behind the guidance; this describes the process (P84).
units.anchor: results from the Student Pulse Survey regarding GenAI, feedback from faculty in various departments
units.policy: Discussions were informed by feedback provided during a special session of the fall meeting of the Academic Senate, results from the Student Pulse Survey regarding GenAI, feedback from faculty in various departments, and Divisional Council discussions related to the rollout of GenAI offerings to the broader campus.

units.why: The university supplies a licensed tool, Google Gemini, with 'data protections through UC Berkeley agreements'. This is an institution-wide tool (P92), not a single course tool (P17).
units.anchor: provided campus-wide access to Google Gemini
units.policy: On June 10th, UC Berkeley provided campus-wide access to Google Gemini — which includes data protections through UC Berkeley agreements with Google — to address privacy and security concerns related to the use of GenAI tools on campus.

units.why: Frames the guidance as neutral on 'whether or not to use' GenAI, leaving the choice to courses: P04.
units.anchor: explore whether or not to use these technologies in their courses
units.policy: Our goal is to help support the academic community as they explore whether or not to use these technologies in their courses.

units.why: Reminds faculty of 'their authority over courses and curriculum', so the instructor decides (P04).
units.anchor: remind faculty of their authority over courses and curriculum
units.policy: Faculty have authority over their courses and curriculum.

units.why: The same sentence also says 'academic expectations should be established in the course syllabus': a direction to state expectations in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: academic expectations should be established in the course syllabus
units.policy: Academic expectations should be established in the course syllabus.

units.why: Says students must understand that 'GenAI hasn't changed the baseline expectations of work'. This reaffirms existing standards; nearest is P29 but it only partly fits.
units.anchor: GenAI hasn't changed the baseline expectations of work in our academic disciplines
units.policy: it is important to ensure that students understand that GenAI hasn't changed the baseline expectations of work in our academic disciplines.
units.fit_note: Says baseline academic expectations are unchanged by GenAI and that students should be told so; it does not state that students own their work.

units.why: Recommends ('we recommend') that every instructor include a syllabus statement on GenAI: P09 with modality should.
units.anchor: we recommend that all faculty include a clear statement on their syllabus
units.policy: we recommend that all faculty include a clear statement on their syllabus about course expectations regarding the use of Google Gemini or any other GenAI tool for course-related work.

units.why: Gives the reason for a syllabus statement: without one students 'may be more likely to use these technologies inappropriately'. Assigned P09, the rule it justifies.
units.anchor: students may be more likely to use these technologies inappropriately
units.policy: In the absence of such a statement, students may be more likely to use these technologies inappropriately or fail to utilize them effectively as a learning tool.

units.why: Says the document is provisional ('we anticipate that this document will evolve'): P54.
units.anchor: we anticipate that this document will evolve
units.policy: As technology and best practices continue to evolve, we anticipate that this document will evolve.

units.why: Describes systemwide recommendations that each Divisional Senate will decide whether to adopt; it explains who will make future instruction policy and how (P84 over P85, since it is about the policy-making process).
units.anchor: Divisional Senates will determine what recommendations to adopt in the area of instruction
units.policy: the systemwide Academic Senate AI Workgroup is finalizing a set of recommendations, including recommendations for instruction, that will be disseminated to all campuses with the expectation that Divisional Senates will determine what recommendations to adopt in the area of instruction

units.why: Says the guidance is a 'starting point for faculty to build and implement the policies that work best in their classrooms', leaving the rule to each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: a starting point for faculty to build and implement the policies that work best in
units.policy: These are not meant to be exhaustive, but rather to provide a starting point for faculty to build and implement the policies that work best in their classrooms.

units.why: Points faculty to GenAI resources and a teaching guide, i.e. support for faculty learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: a set of GenAI resources with an updated teaching guide
units.policy: Research, Teaching, & Learning has a set of GenAI resources with an updated teaching guide that faculty wishing to further explore the use of GenAI in their teaching may find helpful.

units.why: Invites faculty to book a 'confidential, non-evaluative' consultation about GenAI in their courses: faculty support (P63).
units.anchor: consider scheduling a consultation with an educational developer
units.policy: consider scheduling a consultation with an educational developer in the Center for Teaching and Learning.

units.why: Tells instructors to weigh arguments before choosing; the choice is theirs (P04), modality should.
units.anchor: Instructors should carefully evaluate the arguments for and against the use of GenAI before choosing
units.policy: Instructors should carefully evaluate the arguments for and against the use of GenAI before choosing a policy for their course.

units.why: Gives a reason to prohibit GenAI: it 'short-circuits the learning process' because students may not develop their own abilities. Skill-building rationale (P41).
units.anchor: Use of GenAI on assignments short-circuits the learning process.

units.why: Argues that without manual practice students 'may not be able to learn to judge the quality' of output: the novices-need-fundamentals argument (P42).
units.anchor: students may not be able to learn to judge the quality of a GenAI’s output
units.policy: Without learning to accomplish tasks manually, students may not be able to learn to judge the quality of a GenAI’s output.

units.why: Names an ethical objection to tools 'trained on unlicensed human work'; an ethics concern (P53 over P52, since it is an ethical claim, not about output ownership).
units.anchor: Using GenAI tools that were trained on unlicensed human work is ethically questionable.

units.why: States that tools 'fabricate information', a warning that output may be wrong (P31).
units.anchor: GenAI tools sometimes fabricate information, delivering false statements even when they appear to be citing
units.policy: GenAI tools sometimes fabricate information, delivering false statements even when they appear to be citing published work.

units.why: Names bias 'based on their training data' as a harm of GenAI (P53).
units.anchor: GenAI tools produce products that can be biased based on their training data and the
units.policy: GenAI tools produce products that can be biased based on their training data and the organizations that oversee the training.

units.why: Names 'adverse environmental impacts' as an argument for prohibition (P53).
units.anchor: resulting in adverse environmental impacts in terms of emissions and disruptions to natural habitats
units.policy: Some GenAI tools require substantial amounts of energy to run and are sustained by extensive physical infrastructure, resulting in adverse environmental impacts in terms of emissions and disruptions to natural habitats.

units.why: Argument for allowing GenAI: use is 'already ubiquitous'. It gives context, not a rule; nearest P87 fits only partly because it argues from prevalence.
units.anchor: The use of GenAI tools is already ubiquitous, and students likely use these tools in
units.policy: The use of GenAI tools is already ubiquitous, and students likely use these tools in other contexts.
units.fit_note: Argues from prevalence of use, not from a learning benefit.

units.why: Names a benefit of GenAI for research and information gathering; benefit statement (P87).
units.anchor: Students may benefit from using GenAI tools for research to guide the process of information-gathering
units.policy: Students may benefit from using GenAI tools for research to guide the process of information-gathering and contextualization.

units.why: Says GenAI 'may help' writing by 'correcting grammatical errors and providing real-time critical feedback'. A benefit statement (P87); P91 is the permission itself, which this is not.
units.anchor: GenAI tools may help students learn to write more effectively by correcting grammatical errors and
units.policy: GenAI tools may help students learn to write more effectively by correcting grammatical errors and providing real-time critical feedback.

units.why: Names the benefit of speeding up 'data processing and programming tasks'. A benefit statement (P87), not a rule.
units.anchor: accelerate data processing and programming tasks
units.policy: GenAI tools can accelerate data processing and programming tasks so students can focus on other relevant tasks or concepts.

units.why: Names the benefit for 'non-native speakers' via translation: benefit statement (P87) with an access flavor.
units.anchor: GenAI tools may help non-native speakers communicate more effectively by aiding in translation and providing
units.policy: GenAI tools may help non-native speakers communicate more effectively by aiding in translation and providing guidance on potential points of confusion.

units.why: Argues for encouraging 'campus-approved GenAI tools' for data protection and lower climate impact: use university-approved tools (P92).
units.anchor: Encouraging students to use campus-approved GenAI tools
units.policy: Encouraging students to use campus-approved GenAI tools ensures that students take advantage of the enhanced data protection in these tools and potentially lowers the climate impact.

units.why: Career argument for encouraging or requiring GenAI: 'Students need to learn how to effectively utilize GenAI tools to prepare for their future careers' (P44).
units.anchor: Students need to learn how to effectively utilize GenAI tools to prepare for their future
units.policy: GenAI tools are pervasive in the workforce. Students need to learn how to effectively utilize GenAI tools to prepare for their future careers.

units.why: Names 'innovative teaching methods' enabled by GenAI as a benefit (P87).
units.anchor: GenAI tools may lead to innovative teaching methods, such as interaction with virtual teaching aids
units.policy: GenAI tools may lead to innovative teaching methods, such as interaction with virtual teaching aids or debating alternative perspectives.

units.why: Argues required use gives 'hands-on experience' so students learn GenAI's limits: teaching effective use (P44).
units.anchor: Provides hands-on experience so students understand the deficiencies and limitations of GenAI tools.

units.why: Names critical evaluation and 'the appropriate use of prompting' as reasons to require GenAI. P93 fits only the prompting part; P44 chosen for the argument that effective use is taught.
units.anchor: critically evaluate GenAI output, teaching students the appropriate use of prompting
units.policy: Supports students in learning how to critically evaluate GenAI output, teaching students the appropriate use of prompting and co-learning with GenAI.

units.why: Says required use 'enables equitable access to GenAI through a clear pedagogical structure': an equity argument (P51).
units.anchor: Enables equitable access to GenAI through a clear pedagogical structure.

units.why: Offers three sample statements that instructors adapt: a template set with the choice left to instructors (P05 as it names tiers).
units.anchor: Instructors should modify them to fit their course requirements.
units.policy: We provide three sample statements. Instructors should modify them to fit their course requirements.

units.why: Describes the three templates (Full AI, Some AI, No AI) as spanning most to least GenAI use: the named-tiers structure (P05).
units.anchor: The three statements include the two extremes, with the most and least GenAI use.

units.why: Anticipates instructors mixing allowances and prohibitions; the rule is set per instructor (P04).
units.anchor: instructors will choose a different combination of GenAI allowances and prohibitions
units.policy: it is likely that instructors will choose a different combination of GenAI allowances and prohibitions.

units.why: The Full AI sample says 'Students will be required to use GenAI tools provided by the instructor', so AI use is built into the work (P79). P17 also touches instructor-provided tools; P79 chosen as the core is the requirement.
units.anchor: Students will be required to use GenAI tools provided by the instructor to complete assignments.
units.policy: This is a GenAI-required course. Students will be required to use GenAI tools provided by the instructor to complete assignments.

units.why: Full AI sample: other tools allowed 'unless specifically prohibited', a permit-by-default rule (P02).
units.anchor: Students may also use other GenAI tools unless specifically prohibited.

units.why: Full AI sample: exams may bar GenAI, 'clearly identified... in the syllabus'. An assessment carve-out (P22).
units.anchor: assignments in this class (e.g., exams) where the use of GenAI is not permitted
units.policy: There may be assignments in this class (e.g., exams) where the use of GenAI is not permitted, and these will be clearly identified, where appropriate, in the syllabus.

units.why: Some AI sample: 'enables limited uses' but 'prohibits broad use' that would be plagiarism if human-authored. A middle default that fits neither P01 nor P02, so P05 (a named middle tier). It also applies a human-author test (P45).
units.anchor: enables limited uses of GenAI tools but also prohibits broad use of them
units.policy: This course enables limited uses of GenAI tools but also prohibits broad use of them in cases that would be considered plagiaristic if the tool’s output had been composed by a human author.
units.fit_note: Also applies the 'as if a human author composed it' test, which is P45.

units.why: Instructors 'may require' a short in-person oral or paper exam when unauthorized use is suspected: a check of understanding (P34), chosen over P81 because it is not a reporting procedure.
units.anchor: may require you to complete a short, in-person examination orally or on paper
units.policy: If unauthorized GenAI use on a particular assessment is suspected, the instructors may require you to complete a short, in-person examination orally or on paper, related to the content and skills tested in the original assessment.

units.why: Some AI permitted use: research 'similar to search engines'. Search-like use to understand is closest to P12.
units.anchor: perform research in ways similar to search engines such as Google
units.policy: It may be used to perform research in ways similar to search engines such as Google, and for other functions attendant to completing an assignment.
units.fit_note: Search-engine-like research and other 'attendant functions', not specifically concept tutoring.

units.why: Allows GenAI as a writing assistant 'for correcting grammar and spelling' and synonym suggestion: the editing permission (P91).
units.anchor: writing assistant in its capacity as a word processor
units.policy: It may be used as a writing assistant in its capacity as a word processor, such as Word or Pages, i.e., for correcting grammar and spelling, and other functions like synonym suggestion.

units.why: Allows translation 'for consultation purposes'; a prose-specific rule (P18). The ban on presenting it as one's own is coded separately.
units.anchor: It may be used as translation software for consultation purposes
units.policy: It may be used as translation software for consultation purposes; you should never present the GenAI translation as your own text.

units.why: Bars presenting an AI translation 'as your own text': AI-generated text may not be submitted as one's own (P19).
units.anchor: you should never present the GenAI translation as your own text.

units.why: Tells students to cite translation software, an acknowledgement requirement (P24).
units.anchor: Remember to cite the translation software.

units.why: Calls pasting problem text into a GenAI tool 'cheating': a ban on feeding assignment text to AI (P20), also classified as misconduct (P36). P20 chosen as the behavior banned.
units.anchor: Copying any text directly from a homework or lab problem into a GenAI tool is
units.policy: Copying any text directly from a homework or lab problem into a GenAI tool is considered cheating.

units.why: Allows students to 'break problems into steps and paraphrase' them for the tool: a narrow permitted use on problems. Nearest P12 fits only partly.
units.anchor: Students, however, are permitted to break problems into steps and paraphrase those steps in their
units.policy: Students, however, are permitted to break problems into steps and paraphrase those steps in their own words.
units.fit_note: Permits asking AI about a problem when rephrased in the student's own words; not about tutoring on concepts.

units.why: Where AI is allowed, the assignment asks for 'an acknowledgement' plus the 'prompts and outputs'. Disclosure (P24) with prompt and output detail (P25); P25 chosen since prompts and outputs are named.
units.anchor: include an acknowledgement of your use of any type of GenAI in your submitted work
units.policy: When assignments in the course permit or incorporate the use of GenAI tools, the assignment will ask you to include an acknowledgement of your use of any type of GenAI in your submitted work and share the prompts and outputs utilized at the time of submission.

units.why: Gives a template acknowledgement naming the system, use, prompts, and how output was used: tool, prompt and output citation (P25).
units.anchor: I acknowledge the use of [insert AI system(s) and link] to [specific use of GenAI].
units.policy: I acknowledge the use of [insert AI system(s) and link] to [specific use of GenAI]. The prompts used include [list of prompts]. The output from these prompts was used to [explain the use].

units.why: Template that allows AI for some assignment types with citation and not others: a use table per assessment (P05).
units.anchor: GenAI tools may be used for [assignment types A, B, and C] with appropriate citation
units.policy: GenAI tools may be used for [assignment types A, B, and C] with appropriate citation, but not for [assignment types D, E, and F].

units.why: Template line barring GenAI 'for any purpose' in a list the instructor completes: the instructor sets situations (P04).
units.anchor: GenAI tools may not be used for any purpose in the following situations
units.policy: GenAI tools may not be used for any purpose in the following situations: [provide complete list].

units.why: Sample bans composing any part of submitted work with AI (P19).
units.anchor: The software may not be used to compose any part of the submitted assignment.

units.why: Bars using GenAI to 'summarize, generate, or interpret any thoughts' in the student's work; the thinking must be the student's (P32).
units.anchor: should not be used to summarize, generate, or interpret any thoughts present in any of
units.policy: The use of GenAI tools such as ChatGPT or equivalent should not be used to summarize, generate, or interpret any thoughts present in any of your work.

units.why: Uses the human-author test: GenAI 'should never be employed' where it would be plagiarism if human. AI is treated like a human source under existing rules (P45).
units.anchor: GenAI should never be employed for a use that would constitute plagiarism if the GenAI
units.policy: GenAI should never be employed for a use that would constitute plagiarism if the GenAI source were a human or organizational author.

units.why: Says having another entity write 'any substantive portion' is against integrity policy and includes 'using GenAI tools': AI-produced work counts as misconduct (P36). P19 describes the act; this unit frames it through integrity policy.
units.anchor: is against academic integrity policies, and can include hiring a person or a company
units.policy: Having another person/entity do the writing of any substantive portion of an assignment for you is against academic integrity policies, and can include hiring a person or a company to write essays and drafts and/or other assignments, research-based or otherwise, and using GenAI tools.

units.why: No AI sample: 'prohibit the use of any GenAI tools or automated services' during class, assignments and exams. The default rule is a ban (P01).
units.anchor: we have chosen to prohibit the use of any GenAI tools or automated services
units.policy: we have chosen to prohibit the use of any GenAI tools or automated services during class sessions and when completing assignments or exams.

units.why: No AI sample gives its reason: 'active engagement, students' knowledge acquisition, and the development of critical thinking skills'; the skill-building rationale (P41).
units.anchor: we prioritize active engagement, students’ knowledge acquisition, and the development of critical thinking skills.

units.why: No AI sample extends the ban to 'brainstorming, drafting, analysis, editing'; helping uses are banned as well. P01 states the general prohibition and P21 only covers debug/proofread.
units.anchor: GenAI use is not permitted in any aspect of completing work that is part of
units.policy: GenAI use is not permitted in any aspect of completing work that is part of an assignment, including brainstorming, drafting, analysis, editing, or generation of figures or images.

units.why: In the No AI sample, suspected unauthorized use lets the instructor require a short in-person oral or paper exam: a check of understanding (P34). Coded separately from the Some AI wording since this is a different sample statement.
units.anchor: the instructor may require you to complete a short, in-person examination orally or on paper
units.policy: If unauthorized AI use on a particular assessment is suspected, the instructor may require you to complete a short, in-person examination orally or on paper, related to the content and skills tested in the original assessment.

units.why: Tells faculty to 'actively engage students in discussions' about GenAI in the course: explaining and discussing the rules with students (P66).
units.anchor: Faculty should actively engage students in discussions about topics relevant to the use of GenAI
units.policy: Faculty should actively engage students in discussions about topics relevant to the use of GenAI in the specific course.

units.why: Suggested discussion topic 'How to properly cite GenAI sources': instructors discuss citation with students (P66).
units.anchor: How to properly cite GenAI sources
units.policy: Instructors should discuss how to properly cite GenAI sources with students.

units.why: Suggested discussion topic on 'Ethical and legal considerations around the training data': ethics and IP raised for class discussion (P66).
units.anchor: Ethical and legal considerations around the training data and application of GenAI
units.policy: Instructors should discuss ethical and legal considerations around the training data and application of GenAI.

units.why: Suggested discussion topic 'Environmental impact of GenAI' (P66).
units.anchor: Environmental impact of GenAI
units.policy: Instructors should discuss the environmental impact of GenAI with students.

units.why: Suggested discussion topic 'Reasons GenAI usage could be detrimental to learning': instructors explain the learning case (P66).
units.anchor: Reasons GenAI usage could be detrimental to learning
units.policy: Instructors should discuss reasons GenAI usage could be detrimental to learning.

units.why: Suggested discussion topic 'Data protection aspects of using GenAI tools' (P66).
units.anchor: Data protection aspects of using GenAI tools
units.policy: Instructors should discuss data protection aspects of using GenAI tools.

units.why: Suggested discussion topic 'Potential bias produced by GenAI' (P66).
units.anchor: Potential bias produced by GenAI
units.policy: Instructors should discuss potential bias produced by GenAI.

units.why: Suggested discussion topic 'Identifying inconsistencies or errors in GenAI output' (P66).
units.anchor: Identifying inconsistencies or errors in GenAI output
units.policy: Instructors should discuss identifying inconsistencies or errors in GenAI output.

units.why: Suggested discussion topic 'Enforcement mechanisms of GenAI use prohibitions': telling students how bans are enforced (P66).
units.anchor: Enforcement mechanisms of GenAI use prohibitions
units.policy: Instructors should discuss enforcement mechanisms of GenAI use prohibitions.

units.why: Instructors should 'ensure that students have access to the necessary computing resources' when they require AI: equitable access (P51).
units.anchor: instructors should ensure that students have access to the necessary computing resources
units.policy: For any assignments where the instructor encourages or requires the use of GenAI tools, instructors should ensure that students have access to the necessary computing resources to run those GenAI tools.

units.why: Makes the instructor responsible for providing access to non-campus tools they require, so students need not pay (P51).
units.anchor: it is the instructor's responsibility to provide access to those resources
units.policy: If non-campus-sanctioned resources are required, it is the instructor's responsibility to provide access to those resources.

units.why: Syllabus should outline acceptable use of non-campus and instructor-provided tools: a syllabus statement (P09).
units.anchor: The syllabus should clearly outline the acceptable use of non-campus and instructor-provided GenAI tools.

units.why: Where AI is permitted but not required, instructors should prevent an 'unfair advantage' from external tools: equitable access (P51).
units.anchor: ensure that access to external tools does not provide an unfair advantage
units.policy: the instructor should make a reasonable effort to ensure that access to external tools does not provide an unfair advantage.

units.why: Tells students to include an in-text citation for GenAI content: disclosure by citation (P24).
units.anchor: Include an in-text citation when incorporating content from a GenAI tool into your academic paper.

units.why: Says reference entries must give 'publication date (if available), title, model, and URL': citation details of tool, model and date (P25).
units.anchor: provide the publication date (if available), title, model, and URL
units.policy: In your reference list, provide the full details of the source. Since ChatGPT is an online tool, provide the publication date (if available), title, model, and URL:

units.why: Tells students to follow the professor's or publication's format for citations, deferring to the course's rules (P78).
units.anchor: follow the guidelines provided by your professor or the publication's style guide
units.policy: Always follow the guidelines provided by your professor or the publication's style guide for precise formatting.
units.fit_note: Directs citation format specifically, not AI rules generally.

units.why: Says 'there are no validated GenAI detection tools': detectors are unreliable (P39).
units.anchor: there are no validated GenAI detection tools
units.policy: GenAI detection tools are increasingly less accurate; there are no validated GenAI detection tools.

units.why: Instructors with AI-free work should consider the listed alternatives (integrity statement, proctoring, interviews): redesigning assessment in response to AI (P35).
units.anchor: where GenAI is not permitted should consider adopting one or more of the following solutions
units.policy: assignments or learning activities where GenAI is not permitted should consider adopting one or more of the following solutions:

units.why: Suggests a 'Written Statement of Academic Integrity' as an enforcement aid. Nearest P95 (ground limits in honesty) fits only partly.
units.anchor: As a member of the UC Berkeley community, I act with honesty, integrity, and respect
units.policy: Written Statement of Academic Integrity: As a member of the UC Berkeley community, I act with honesty, integrity, and respect for others.
units.fit_note: A suggested pledge students sign as a deterrent; the type is about honesty as the reason for AI rules.

units.why: Lists 'In-person proctored exams/activities' as a solution where GenAI is not permitted: shifting to proctored assessment (P33).
units.anchor: In-person proctored exams/activities
units.policy: Where GenAI is not permitted, instructors should consider in-person proctored exams or activities.

units.why: Lists an interview or oral exam where students 'are graded on an explanation of their work': checks understanding (P34).
units.anchor: students are graded on an explanation of their work
units.policy: An additional interview component (or oral exam) to an assignment where students are graded on an explanation of their work.

units.why: Encourages instructors to 'directly state the consequences of cheating and their reporting process': penalties stated in advance (P37).
units.anchor: directly state the consequences of cheating and their reporting process
units.policy: Instructors are encouraged to directly state the consequences of cheating and their reporting process as part of the AI Policy.

units.why: Example consequence: report to the Center for Student Conduct and redo in person. Concrete penalty and reporting (P37).
units.anchor: will be reported to the Center for Student Conduct and will be required to redo
units.policy: a student who is suspected of violating the GenAI policy will be reported to the Center for Student Conduct and will be required to redo the assignment in person.

units.why: Code of Student Conduct excerpt defining cheating as using prohibited or inappropriate materials. AI is not named, but this is the integrity rule that unauthorized AI falls under (P36).
units.anchor: using or attempting to use materials, or assisting others in using materials that are prohibited
units.policy: Cheating includes fraud, deceit, or dishonesty in an academic assignment, or using or attempting to use materials, or assisting others in using materials that are prohibited or inappropriate in the context of the academic assignment in question.
units.fit_note: AI is not named; the definition is the general misconduct rule to which AI rules attach.

units.why: Code of Conduct definition of plagiarism, including self-plagiarism. AI is not mentioned; it is part of the integrity framework (P36 only partly).
units.anchor: Plagiarism includes use of intellectual material produced by another person without acknowledging its source.
units.fit_note: Defines plagiarism generally; AI is not mentioned.

units.why: Code of Conduct definition of false information and fabrication. A general conduct rule that does not mention AI and fits no AI type well.
units.anchor: fabricating or altering information and presenting it as legitimate
units.policy: Furnishing false information, failing to identify oneself honestly, fabricating or altering information and presenting it as legitimate, or providing false or misleading information to an instructor or any other University official in an academic context.
units.uncovered_note: General conduct definition of false information, fabrication and misrepresentation to instructors, with no reference to AI.

units.why: Says students 'are responsible for clarifying the standards and expectations' of their departments: students must find out the rules that apply (P78).
units.anchor: students are responsible for clarifying the standards and expectations of their individual departments
units.policy: Individual departments at the University of California, Berkeley may have differing expectations for students, and therefore students are responsible for clarifying the standards and expectations of their individual departments.

units.why: Acknowledges departments 'may have differing expectations': units may set their own rules (P85).
units.anchor: Individual departments at the University of California, Berkeley may have differing expectations for students

documents.title: Communicating Course Policies and Talking with Students
documents.summary: Center for Teaching & Learning page on communicating GenAI course policies. It repeats the Senate's three sample statements, shows example statements from Berkeley instructors in mathematics, public policy, STS and a Social Sciences checkbox template, and advises instructors to explain their reasons to students.
documents.stance_why: The page presents sample syllabus statements that 'span a range of approaches, from fully integrating GenAI into coursework to prohibiting it entirely' and urges instructors to adapt them, so it sets no stance itself and lists tiers.

units.why: Says instructors are 'expected to make informed decisions' about GenAI aligned with their pedagogical goals: the instructor decides (P04).
units.anchor: instructors are increasingly expected to make informed decisions
units.policy: instructors are increasingly expected to make informed decisions about how these tools align with their pedagogical values and goals.

units.why: States the purpose of the page: to set expectations and 'foster a culture of transparency, integrity, and shared responsibility'; a framework statement of purpose (P56).
units.anchor: foster a culture of transparency, integrity, and shared responsibility
units.policy: it offers a comprehensive overview of how to set expectations, open up dialogue, and foster a culture of transparency, integrity, and shared responsibility.

units.why: Tells instructors to communicate even without a final stance because 'students are already wondering how (or if) they’re allowed to use it': state expectations (P09).
units.anchor: students are already wondering how (or if) they’re allowed to use it
units.policy: Even if you haven’t finalized your stance on generative AI in your course, students are already wondering how (or if) they’re allowed to use it.

units.why: Says a clear course policy should explain 'not only what is allowed, but also why': explaining the rules to students (P66).
units.anchor: understand not only what is allowed, but also why
units.policy: A clearly stated course policy on GenAI use helps ensure that students understand not only what is allowed, but also why.

units.why: Says policies should be 'grounded in pedagogical reasoning and tied to the specific learning goals': AI decisions follow learning objectives (P83).
units.anchor: grounded in pedagogical reasoning and tied to the specific learning goals of the course
units.policy: Policies are more effective when they are grounded in pedagogical reasoning and tied to the specific learning goals of the course.

units.why: Lists benefits of a transparent policy (less anxiety, supports integrity, reflection). A rationale for communicating; closest P66 but it fits only partly.
units.anchor: reduces student anxiety, supports academic integrity
units.policy: A transparent policy also reduces student anxiety, supports academic integrity, and allows space for students to reflect on the ethical and disciplinary dimensions of GenAI use.
units.fit_note: Gives benefits of a transparent policy rather than telling instructors to explain their reasoning.

units.why: Says a policy should 'invite students into a shared conversation' about how, when and why. This is discussing the rules with students (P66); P67 (co-creating) is not stated since the policy is not set jointly.
units.anchor: should invite students into a shared conversation about how, when, and why
units.policy: a good GenAI policy should not merely act as a set of rules but should invite students into a shared conversation about how, when, and why certain technologies can (or shouldn’t) be used in the service of learning.

units.why: Sample statements are for adapting: the instructor chooses (P04).
units.anchor: Instructors are encouraged to adapt these to their specific course context
units.policy: Instructors are encouraged to adapt these to their specific course context and instructional priorities.

units.why: Describes the Senate samples as a range from full integration to prohibition: named tiers (P05).
units.anchor: They span a range of approaches, from fully integrating GenAI into coursework to prohibiting it
units.policy: They span a range of approaches, from fully integrating GenAI into coursework to prohibiting it entirely.

units.why: Full AI sample: 'Students will be required to use GenAI tools provided by the instructor', AI built into the work (P79).
units.anchor: Students will be required to use GenAI tools provided by the instructor to complete assignments.
units.policy: This is a GenAI-required course. Students will be required to use GenAI tools provided by the instructor to complete assignments.

units.why: Full AI sample: other tools allowed 'unless specifically prohibited' (P02).
units.anchor: Students may also use other GenAI tools unless specifically prohibited.

units.why: Full AI sample: exams may bar GenAI, 'clearly identified in the syllabus' (P22).
units.anchor: assignments in this class (e.g., exams) where the use of GenAI is not permitted
units.policy: There may be assignments in this class (e.g., exams) where the use of GenAI is not permitted, and these will be clearly identified in the syllabus.

units.why: Some AI sample: 'enables limited uses' but 'prohibits broad use' that would be plagiarism if human-authored. A middle tier (P05) with a human-author test (P45).
units.anchor: enables limited uses of GenAI tools but also prohibits broad use of them
units.policy: This course enables limited uses of GenAI tools but also prohibits broad use of them in cases that would be considered plagiaristic if the tool’s output had been composed by a human author.
units.fit_note: Also applies the 'as if a human author composed it' test, which is P45.

units.why: Some AI sample: suspected unauthorized use lets instructors require a short in-person oral or paper exam: a check of understanding (P34).
units.anchor: may require you to complete a short, in-person examination orally or on paper
units.policy: If unauthorized GenAI use on a particular assessment is suspected, the instructors may require you to complete a short, in-person examination orally or on paper, related to the content and skills tested in the original assessment.

units.why: Some AI permitted use: research 'similar to search engines'; closest P12.
units.anchor: perform research in ways similar to search engines such as Google
units.policy: It may be used to perform research in ways similar to search engines such as Google, and for other functions attendant to completing an assignment.
units.fit_note: Search-engine-like research and other 'attendant functions', not specifically concept tutoring.

units.why: Allows GenAI as a writing assistant 'for correcting grammar and spelling': editing permission (P91).
units.anchor: writing assistant in its capacity as a word processor
units.policy: It may be used as a writing assistant in its capacity as a word processor, such as Word or Pages, i.e., for correcting grammar and spelling, and other functions like synonym suggestion.

units.why: Allows translation 'for consultation purposes' and bars presenting it as one's own text. A prose rule (P18); coded as one rule with its limit.
units.anchor: It may be used as translation software for consultation purposes
units.policy: It may be used as translation software for consultation purposes; you should never present the GenAI translation as your own text.

units.why: Calls pasting problem text into a GenAI tool 'cheating': a ban on feeding assignment text to AI (P20).
units.anchor: Copying any text directly from a homework or lab problem into a GenAI tool is
units.policy: Copying any text directly from a homework or lab problem into a GenAI tool is considered cheating.

units.why: Allows students to 'break problems into steps and paraphrase' them: a narrow permitted use. Nearest P12 fits only partly.
units.anchor: Students, however, are permitted to break problems into steps and paraphrase those steps in their
units.policy: Students, however, are permitted to break problems into steps and paraphrase those steps in their own words.
units.fit_note: Permits asking AI about a problem when rephrased in the student's own words; not about tutoring on concepts.

units.why: Where AI is allowed, an 'acknowledgement' plus 'prompts and outputs' are requested. Disclosure (P24) with prompt and output detail (P25); P25 chosen.
units.anchor: include an acknowledgement of your use of any type of GenAI in your submitted work
units.policy: When assignments in the course permit or incorporate the use of GenAI tools, the assignment will ask you to include an acknowledgement of your use of any type of GenAI in your submitted work and share the prompts and outputs utilized at the time of submission.

units.why: Template acknowledgement naming system, use, prompts and how output was used (P25).
units.anchor: I acknowledge the use of [insert AI system(s) and link] to [specific use of GenAI].
units.policy: I acknowledge the use of [insert AI system(s) and link] to [specific use of GenAI]. The prompts used include [list of prompts]. The output from these prompts was used to [explain the use].

units.why: Template that allows AI for some assignment types with citation and not others: a use table per assessment (P05).
units.anchor: GenAI tools may be used for [assignment types A, B, and C] with appropriate citation
units.policy: GenAI tools may be used for [assignment types A, B, and C] with appropriate citation, but not for [assignment types D, E, and F].

units.why: Some AI sample: 'may not be used for any purpose in any exam situation': no AI on exams (P22).
units.anchor: GenAI tools may not be used for any purpose in any exam situation.

units.why: Sample bans composing any part of submitted work with AI (P19).
units.anchor: The software may not be used to compose any part of the submitted assignment.

units.why: Bars using GenAI to 'summarize, generate, or interpret any thoughts' in the student's work: the student stays the thinker (P32).
units.anchor: should not be used to summarize, generate, or interpret any thoughts present in any of
units.policy: The use of GenAI tools such as ChatGPT or equivalent should not be used to summarize, generate, or interpret any thoughts present in any of your work.

units.why: Human-author test: AI treated like a human source under plagiarism rules (P45).
units.anchor: GenAI should never be employed for a use that would constitute plagiarism if the GenAI
units.policy: GenAI should never be employed for a use that would constitute plagiarism if the GenAI source were a human or organizational author.

units.why: Says having another entity write 'any substantive portion' is against integrity policy and includes 'using GenAI tools': AI-written work as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: is against academic integrity policies, and can include hiring a person or a company
units.policy: Having another person/entity do the writing of any substantive portion of an assignment for you is against academic integrity policies, and can include hiring a person or a company to write essays and drafts and/or other assignments, research-based or otherwise, and using GenAI tools.

units.why: No AI sample: 'prohibit the use of any GenAI tools or automated services' (P01).
units.anchor: we have chosen to prohibit the use of any GenAI tools or automated services
units.policy: we have chosen to prohibit the use of any GenAI tools or automated services during class sessions and when completing assignments or exams.

units.why: No AI sample gives its reason: 'active engagement, students' knowledge acquisition, and the development of critical thinking skills' (P41).
units.anchor: we prioritize active engagement, students’ knowledge acquisition, and the development of critical thinking skills.

units.why: No AI sample extends the ban to 'brainstorming, drafting, analysis, editing'. P01 states the general prohibition.
units.anchor: GenAI use is not permitted in any aspect of completing work that is part of
units.policy: GenAI use is not permitted in any aspect of completing work that is part of an assignment, including brainstorming, drafting, analysis, editing, or generation of figures or images.

units.why: No AI sample: suspected use lets the instructor require a short in-person exam: understanding check (P34). Separate unit as it is a different sample statement.
units.anchor: the instructor may require you to complete a short, in-person examination orally or on paper
units.policy: If unauthorized AI use on a particular assessment is suspected, the instructor may require you to complete a short, in-person examination orally or on paper, related to the content and skills tested in the original assessment.

units.why: Points to the full Senate guidance for risks, access, citation and enforcement; a cross-reference to the university framework (P56).
units.anchor: full guidance also addresses risks and limitations of GenAI
units.policy: The Academic Senate’s full guidance also addresses

units.why: A MATH instructor's example statement bars GenAI for polls, exams and 'most HWs': a restrictive default for the course (P01 only partly, since some HWs specify AI). P01 chosen.
units.anchor: GenAI tools are not allowed to answer polls and when completing exams and most HWs.
units.fit_note: Ban is for most work, with stated exceptions in some HWs.

units.why: Example statement: certain HWs will specify GenAI use for 'calculations, analysis, or generation of figures or images'. Assignment-level required use (P79) with data analysis (P89 only partly).
units.anchor: GenAI (or other online tools) will be specified to use in completing aspects of work
units.policy: In some HWs and investigative parts of the course, GenAI (or other online tools) will be specified to use in completing aspects of work, including calculations, analysis, or generation of figures or images.

units.why: Allows AI for 'grammar, punctuation, and word-smithing' but not for 'generating ideas and the structure of the solutions': editing permission (P91) with a limit.
units.anchor: You can use AI tools for grammar, punctuation, and word-smithing on HWs
units.policy: You can use AI tools for grammar, punctuation, and word-smithing on HWs, or for calculations only as specified in the HWs, but not for generating ideas and the structure of the solutions.

units.why: States that students should use AI 'as a tool, not a replacement for active learning': students remain the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: You need to learn to use AI maturely and as a tool, not a replacement
units.policy: You need to learn to use AI maturely and as a tool, not a replacement for active learning.

units.why: A Public Policy instructor's example statement strongly encourages AI for research: 'If you are not using them yet, you are falling behind'. Default encouraged use (P02).
units.anchor: If you are not using them yet, you are falling behind
units.policy: I am a big proponent of using these tools to increase productivity. If you are not using them yet, you are falling behind

units.why: Tells students to 'confirm everything that goes into your deliverables' because bots make 'creative inferences': verify AI output (P31).
units.anchor: You should confirm everything that goes into your deliverables.

units.why: Suggests paying for the most advanced AI version. It touches cost/access but pushes the opposite way from P51 (no required paid tools); recorded as UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: not paying a modest sum for the most advanced version is a false economy.
units.uncovered_note: Instructor advises students to pay for the best AI tool; this is neither a requirement nor equity protection.

units.why: Bars generative AI for 'ANY writing whatsoever', from rough drafts to copy edits: a prose-specific ban (P18) on AI-produced and edited writing.
units.anchor: You may not use generative AI to do ANY writing whatsoever
units.policy: You may not use generative AI to do ANY writing whatsoever, including the earliest of rough drafts or the latest of copy edits.

units.why: Extends the writing ban to ESL help yet says 'Grammarly is fine', i.e., routine grammar tools are exempt (P100).
units.anchor: Grammarly is fine.
units.policy: Grammarly is fine even though generative AI may not be used for any writing.

units.why: Tells students to 'ask me first' when in doubt: P10.
units.anchor: If you have any doubt about what you may use AI for, ask me first.

units.why: Explains the approach: trusting graduate students to take 'responsibility for their own learning and how AI affects it' (P29 only partly; it explains why the rule is light-touch).
units.anchor: I assume graduate students can take responsibility for their own learning and how AI affects
units.policy: I assume graduate students can take responsibility for their own learning and how AI affects it.
units.fit_note: A rationale for a permissive research use policy, not a rule that students own their work.

units.why: Reason for banning AI writing: 'Writing is part of understanding'. It says doing the work builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: I deplore the use of AI for writing. Writing is part of understanding.
units.policy: Writing is part of understanding.

units.why: An Economics for Policy Makers statement: no AI 'on any part of this course, except for exam preparation'. A default ban (P01) with one exception allowing study use (P14).
units.anchor: You may not use artificial intelligence of any kind on any part of this course
units.policy: You may not use artificial intelligence of any kind on any part of this course, except for exam preparation.

units.why: The exception allows AI for 'exam preparation': a study-aid use (P14).
units.anchor: except for exam preparation
units.policy: AI may be used for exam preparation.

units.why: States that AI on any quiz, resource collection assignment or memo 'will be considered cheating': misconduct classification (P36).
units.anchor: Use of AI on any quiz, resource collection assignment, or memo will be considered cheating.

units.why: Staff say they will not enforce the ban because it is 'fundamentally impossible': declining to police AI use (P60); the unverifiable-control point (P82) is secondary.
units.anchor: We will not attempt to enforce this rule, as we believe that is fundamentally impossible
units.policy: We will not attempt to enforce this rule, as we believe that is fundamentally impossible, but you need to understand that if you break this rule, you are cheating

units.why: Explains the ban: students must 'learn how to do 100% of the work themselves' as the course teaches basic concepts: skill-building rationale (P41).
units.anchor: They need to learn how to do 100% of the work themselves.

units.why: Says without the basics students cannot use AI 'effectively and responsibly': fundamentals first (P42).
units.anchor: if they do not understand the basics fully they will never be able to harness
units.policy: if they do not understand the basics fully they will never be able to harness the power of AI as an assistant effectively and responsibly.

units.why: An STS instructor moves all assessments to 'the classroom on pen and paper and without digital devices': shifting to proctored, unassisted assessment (P33).
units.anchor: done in the classroom on pen and paper and without digital devices
units.policy: All your assessments in this course will be done in the classroom on pen and paper and without digital devices

units.why: Gives evidence from the instructor's experience ('bland, generic, similar-sounding prose') for moving to in-class assessment: evidence on AI's effect on learning (P55).
units.anchor: students were writing bland, generic, similar-sounding prose in their take-home papers
units.policy: I found that students were writing bland, generic, similar-sounding prose in their take-home papers and this is why I have moved to in-class assessments.

units.why: Strongly discourages using AI to do the readings: not formally forbidden ('idea'), so P03.
units.anchor: It is a bad -- in fact, downright terrible -- idea to use AI to
units.policy: It is a bad -- in fact, downright terrible -- idea to use AI to do the readings.

units.why: Direct ban: 'Do not use AI to summarize the readings'. Students must produce their own summary (P19 as AI may not generate the work; P41 is the reason).
units.anchor: Do not use AI to summarize the readings.
units.policy: Do not use AI to summarize the readings. Instead, write a summary of the reading in your own words.

units.why: Encourages AI for comprehension help when stuck on a line or paragraph: tutor use for understanding (P12).
units.anchor: using AI if you have difficulties while reading
units.policy: using AI if you have difficulties while reading -- e.g., if you don't understand a certain line or paragraph -- is actually a great idea.

units.why: Tells students to annotate AI answers 'in your own words': keeps the student the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: annotate your document with this answer
units.policy: when you ask AI a question about comprehension and it provides an answer, annotate your document with this answer but in your own words.

units.why: Ban on doing 'your actual writing using AI': no AI-generated text submitted (P19).
units.anchor: Most important: Do NOT do your actual writing using AI.

units.why: Allows AI feedback on an argument and revision suggestions: writing support (P91).
units.anchor: You can ask AI to comment on your argument and perhaps suggest revisions.

units.why: Strict ban on AI prose in the student's significant writing (P19).
units.anchor: But NEVER let any kind of AI prose into the significant writing that is YOURS.

units.why: Allows brainstorming and scrutinizing an argument (P15) but bans copy-pasting AI text (P19). Anchored on the permission; the ban is coded just before in 'NEVER let any kind of AI prose'.
units.anchor: It is okay to use AI to brainstorm ideas or to scrutinize your argument
units.policy: It is okay to use AI to brainstorm ideas or to scrutinize your argument but never, ever, copy-paste AI text into your writing.

units.why: Explains the writing ban: 'When you outsource the writing, you outsource the thinking' (P41).
units.anchor: When you outsource the writing, you outsource the thinking.

units.why: States that students are 'responsible for the text that you write' and readers may object to LLM text: ownership of submitted text (P29).
units.anchor: you are responsible for the text that you write
units.policy: you are responsible for the text that you write and there are many contexts where your readers may not like that you used LLMs to generate text that was meant to be yours.

units.why: Instructor says policing AI is hard and take-home work no longer assesses learning: AI use cannot be fully controlled or verified (P82).
units.anchor: Policing AI use has become harder and harder
units.policy: Policing AI use has become harder and harder and I find myself unable to assess student learning anymore from take-home assignments

units.why: Explains the policy was written to focus on learning and avoid political position-taking; framing of purpose of the policy (P56 only partly).
units.anchor: I wanted to avoid using the policy to do any kind of political position-taking on
units.policy: I wanted to avoid using the policy to do any kind of political position-taking on AI.
units.fit_note: Explains the author's intent and neutrality, rather than stating principles for AI use.

units.why: Instructor observes students studying from AI-generated summaries rather than their own notes, grounding the advice in an observed effect on learning (P55).
units.anchor: I see students studying out of AI-generated summaries rather than their own notes
units.policy: Even for exams, I see students studying out of AI-generated summaries rather than their own notes on the readings.

units.why: Social Sciences division fallback: absent a syllabus policy 'AI use is entirely banned from student assignments' (P06).
units.anchor: If no policy is specified in a syllabus, it will be presumed that AI use
units.policy: If no policy is specified in a syllabus, it will be presumed that AI use is entirely banned from student assignments.

units.why: Division delegates the decision to each faculty member (P04).
units.anchor: Each faculty member in the Division of Social Sciences will therefore need to decide
units.policy: Each faculty member in the Division of Social Sciences will therefore need to decide what the best policy for students’ AI use in their classes ought to be.

units.why: Division's rationale: AI 'threatens to undermine the learning process itself' by short-circuiting struggle (P41).
units.anchor: AI thus threatens to undermine the learning process itself, by short-circuiting individual struggles to gain
units.policy: AI thus threatens to undermine the learning process itself, by short-circuiting individual struggles to gain insight and knowledge.

units.why: Template premise: no universal approach across disciplines, so rules vary by instructor (P04).
units.anchor: there is not a universal approach that will work for all disciplines across the Division
units.policy: It is based on the idea that there is not a universal approach that will work for all disciplines across the Division.

units.why: Social Sciences checkbox template starts from a ban with checked exceptions: a default ban (P01) built as a table of uses (P05). Chose P05 since the unit introduces the exception checklist.
units.anchor: No Artificial Intelligence tool is permitted for class assignments, with the following exceptions:

units.why: Template exception: grammar and spelling help on completed drafts (P91).
units.anchor: Grammar and/or spelling help (for minor writing assistance on student’s own completed drafts)
units.policy: A template exception may allow grammar and/or spelling help for minor writing assistance on the student's own completed drafts.

units.why: Template exception: substantial editing help on the student's own drafts (P91).
units.anchor: Substantial editing help (suggestions for restructuring student’s own drafts, identifying problems with argument or structure
units.policy: A template exception may allow substantial editing help on the student's own drafts.

units.why: Template exception: generating topics or research questions: idea generation (P15).
units.anchor: Generating topics and/or research questions for a student assignment (including generating options from which a
units.policy: A template exception may allow generating topics and/or research questions for a student assignment.

units.why: Template exception: AI-generated outlines or arguments for the student to complete: idea generation (P15).
units.anchor: Generating outlines or arguments for the student to complete with their own writing
units.policy: A template exception may allow generating outlines or arguments for the student to complete with their own writing.

units.why: Template exception: finding sources and reference materials; research use similar to a search engine (P12).
units.anchor: Identification of relevant information sources and reference materials
units.policy: A template exception may allow identification of relevant information sources and reference materials.
units.fit_note: Finding sources is research assistance, not concept tutoring.

units.why: Template exception: summaries of information and scholarship. Closest is P14 (summaries).
units.anchor: Summaries of relevant information, related scholarship, or similar materials
units.policy: A template exception may allow summaries of relevant information, related scholarship, or similar materials.

units.why: Template exception: AI-written drafts or finished text. It is the most permissive checkbox and directly allows what P19 forbids, so P16-like permissions; nearest is P16 though it concerns prose, hence a fit note.
units.anchor: Writing drafts and/or finished text for part or all of a submitted paper
units.policy: A template exception may allow writing drafts and/or finished text for part or all of a submitted paper.
units.fit_note: Permits AI-written prose for submitted papers, not code.

units.why: Template exception: AI finds data for analysis (P89).
units.anchor: Finding data for analysis
units.policy: A template exception may allow finding data for analysis.

units.why: Template exception: AI analyzes data (P89).
units.anchor: Analyzing data
units.policy: A template exception may allow analyzing data.

units.why: Template exception: AI generates graphs, slides, images. Closest is P89 (visualization), though it extends to slides and images.
units.anchor: Generating visual materials (graphs, slides, images, etc.)
units.policy: A template exception may allow generating visual materials (graphs, slides, images, etc.).
units.fit_note: Includes slides and images beyond data visualization.

units.why: Template exception: AI as interlocutor giving critical feedback before submission (P15 for idea generation; P91 for feedback). Chose P15 as the unit stresses idea generation.
units.anchor: Acting as the intellectual interlocutor with the student for idea generation: providing critical perspectives on
units.policy: A template exception may allow AI to act as an intellectual interlocutor for idea generation, giving critical perspectives and feedback on the student's work before submission.

units.why: Template exception: AI as a study buddy providing quiz activities: study aid (P14).
units.anchor: Acting as a study-buddy for the student, providing supplementary quiz activities to reinforce learning course
units.policy: A template exception may allow AI to act as a study buddy providing supplementary quiz activities.

units.why: Template exception: translating course material into the student's native language (P18).
units.anchor: Translating English-language course material into a student’s native language
units.policy: A template exception may allow translating English-language course material into a student's native language.

units.why: Template exception: translating primary sources into English (P18).
units.anchor: Translating primary source documents in another language into English
units.policy: A template exception may allow translating primary source documents in another language into English.

units.why: Instructors assume no AI beyond the checked exceptions: the rule when something is not explicitly allowed is no AI (P06).
units.anchor: Instructors will assume that students have refrained from using AI except in the allowed (i.e.,
units.policy: Instructors will assume that students have refrained from using AI except in the allowed (i.e., checked) cases.

units.why: Instructors 'may request students sign a statement' on AI use: disclosure with a submission (P24).
units.anchor: Instructors may request students sign a statement that they have not used AI
units.policy: Instructors may request students sign a statement that they have not used AI, or have used it only for allowed purposes.

units.why: On suspicion instructors 'may request... oral and/or documentary evidence' of the student's own work: checking understanding (P34).
units.anchor: may request students provide oral and/or documentary evidence
units.policy: instructors may request students provide oral and/or documentary evidence supporting the claim that this is the student’s own work.

units.why: States concrete possible penalties ('zero for the assignment, failing the course, reporting the student'): penalties stated in advance (P37).
units.anchor: penalties may include: zero for the assignment, failing the course, reporting the student
units.policy: If the instructor finds that the student has abused AI, penalties may include: zero for the assignment, failing the course, reporting the student for violation of academic integrity policies, and/or other penalties at the instructor’s discretion.

units.why: Tells instructors to explain 'not only what is permitted or prohibited, but also why': explaining the rules (P66).
units.anchor: explain not only what is permitted or prohibited, but also why
units.policy: consider making time to explain not only what is permitted or prohibited, but also why you’ve taken that approach and how it connects to the learning in your course.

units.why: Suggests clarifying with students 'whether expectations vary across assignments': each assignment may have its own rule, communicated to students (P11 only partly).
units.anchor: whether expectations vary across assignments
units.policy: Instructors might clarify whether expectations vary across assignments.
units.fit_note: Asks instructors to say whether rules differ by assignment; P11 is about rules not carrying across courses.

units.why: Suggests telling students what to do 'if they are unsure whether a particular use is allowed': ask-when-unsure guidance (P10).
units.anchor: what students should do if they are unsure whether a particular use is allowed
units.policy: Instructors might clarify what students should do if they are unsure whether a particular use is allowed.

units.why: Suggests clarifying how students should 'acknowledge or cite AI use': disclosure expectations (P24).
units.anchor: how you want students to acknowledge or cite AI use
units.policy: Instructors might clarify how they want students to acknowledge or cite AI use.

units.why: Suggests clarifying 'what responsible use looks like in the context of your course': discussing the rules (P66).
units.anchor: what responsible use looks like in the context of your course
units.policy: Instructors might clarify what responsible use looks like in the context of their course.

units.why: Suggests pointing students to 'campus guidance and licensed tools': university-licensed tools (P92).
units.anchor: where students can find campus guidance and licensed tools
units.policy: Instructors might clarify where students can find campus guidance and licensed tools.

units.why: Recommends sharing the Vice Provost's student guide to AI best practices and tools as a conversation starter: AI literacy resource for students (P70).
units.anchor: share the guide with students as a starting point for conversations about AI use
units.policy: You may want to share the guide with students as a starting point for conversations about AI use in your courses.

notes: No school-level or computing-unit policy found (EECS, CDSS, iSchool); course layer deferred. Example statements from non-computing Berkeley instructors on the CTL page (MATH, Public Policy, STS, Social Sciences) are coded as units of the CTL document, not as course-layer documents. Some anchors in lists use the item text as the anchor, with the normalized policy in the policy field.
